		<title>Ice Giant or Magma Ocean World?</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/ice-giant-or-magma-ocean-world/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/ice-giant-or-magma-ocean-world/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 30 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[geophysics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[magma]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[miscibility]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[numerical simulation]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[planetary science]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[supercritical fluids]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31585</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Uranus and Neptune&#8211;known as our system&#8217;s ice giants&#8211;are our least explored planets. Both have received exactly one flyby, from the Voyager 2 spacecraft. The data from those flybys remain our primary source of knowledge about each planet. The traditional model for each planet&#8217;s interior (dating back to before the flybys) consists of three layers: a [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><a href="/tagged/uranus/">Uranus</a> and <a href="/tagged/neptune/">Neptune</a>&#8211;known as our system&#8217;s ice giants&#8211;are our least explored planets. Both have received exactly one flyby, from the Voyager 2 spacecraft. The data from those flybys remain our primary source of knowledge about each planet. The traditional model for each planet&#8217;s interior (dating back to before the flybys) consists of three layers: a rocky core; an icy mantle made up of water, ammonia, and methane; and a hydrogen/helium-rich atmosphere. That structure is one way to match the limited measurements we have from these planets, but, as today&#8217;s <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18219">preprint study</a> points out, it&#8217;s not the only way. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The authors suggest an alternative structure, in which a hydrogen-rich atmosphere overlays a <a href="/tagged/supercritical-fluids/">supercritical</a> magma ocean capable of dissolving hydrogen into heavier, metallic elements. Their suggestion is motivated by several factors. First, objects in the outer solar system&#8211;including Kuiper Belt objects&#8211;have less icy material than originally assumed, which suggests that Uranus and Neptune&#8217;s progenitors wouldn&#8217;t have been so ice-rich, either. Second, our understanding of how &#8220;rocky&#8221; materials respond at the temperatures and pressures found in these planet interiors has evolved. In particular, silicate, hydrogen, and iron are actually <a href="/tagged/miscibility/">miscible</a> at these conditions. That means that discrete sub-layers separated by material type are <em>not</em> as likely.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Using the magma ocean model, the team found compositions for both Uranus and Neptune that conformed well to our limited data about their gravitational and magnetic field properties. Time&#8211;and more data&#8211;will tell as to which interior model best describes these enigmatic giants. (Image credit: <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/uranus-planet-Li41RApUAQA">NASA</a>; research credit: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18219">E. Young et al.</a> (preprint); via <a href="https://gizmodo.com/scientists-think-uranus-and-neptune-may-not-be-the-ice-giants-we-imagined-2000778382?__readwiseLocation=">Gizmodo</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

In this video, they send several careening down a slope into Dan&#8217;s face. Watching the balloons descend and pop is (unsurprisingly) my favorite part. <div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/balloon_face1-1024x576.png" title="The water blob is coming..." alt="The water blob is coming..." /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">It&#8217;s the summertime, so Gav and Dan of the Slow Mo Guys are back to experimenting with giant water balloons. In this video, they send   several careening down a slope into Dan&#8217;s face. Watching the balloons descend and pop is (unsurprisingly) my favorite part. It&#8217;s neat to see how the <a href="/tagged/elasticity/">elasticity</a> of the balloon acts like a beefed-up <a href="/tagged/surface-tension/">surface tension</a> to make this enormous blob of water act like an oversized droplet. (Video and image credit: The Slow Mo Guys)</p>

		<title>Inside an Espresso Bed</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/inside-an-espresso-bed/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/inside-an-espresso-bed/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[coffee]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[When pulling a shot of espresso, there are complicated physics at play. The ground coffee is tamped into a puck-like bed of grains, through which high-temperature, high-pressure water is forced. Here, researchers used X-ray tomography to visualize how and when water moves through the bed, which affects how flavors extract. In a finely ground bed, [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">When pulling a shot of <a href="/tagged/coffee/">espresso</a>, there are complicated physics at play. The ground coffee is tamped into a puck-like bed of grains, through which high-temperature, high-pressure water is forced. Here, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0245167">researchers used</a> X-ray tomography to <a href="/tagged/flow-visualization/">visualize</a> how and when water moves through the bed, which affects how flavors extract.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="1024" height="496" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1-1024x496.png" alt="Composite images of water penetrating a bed of finely ground coffee (left) and a bed of coarsely ground coffee (right)." class="wp-image-30960" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1-1024x496.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1-300x145.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1-768x372.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1.png 1200w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Composite images of water penetrating a bed of finely ground coffee (left) and a bed of coarsely ground coffee (right).</figcaption></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In a finely ground bed, water is relatively slow to penetrate the bed, but moves in fairly uniformly. Water can get into the coarse grind a little faster but does so less uniformly. With the new experimental technique in place, the team is interested in seeing how water temperature affects infiltration and what solids get extracted. (Image credit: top &#8211; <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/white-ceramic-mug-with-coffee-CbBY9Q9m4fY">R. Wicks</a>, experiment &#8211; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0245167">J. Foster et al.</a>; research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0245167">J. Foster et al.</a>; via <a href="https://physicsworld.com/a/coffee-with-a-splash-of-physics-how-to-make-the-most-out-of-your-brew/?nbd_source=3626823&amp;__readwiseLocation=">Physics World</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">For much of the year, Cañon Fiord in the Canadian Arctic lies under ice and snow, but in the summer melt season, colors peek out. Here sea ice and sediment swirl in the fjord in eddies that are kilometers wide. The sediment is largely glacial flour&#8211;rock that&#8217;s been ground into dust by glaciers. It provides critical nutrients  for the marine ecosystem. (Image credit: L. Dauphin; via <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/canon-fiords-whirling-waters/?__readwiseLocation=">NASA Earth Observatory</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-large"><img decoding="async" width="1024" height="683" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main-1024x683.jpg" alt="Satellite image of sea ice and sediment swirling in Cañon Fiord." class="wp-image-30688" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main-1024x683.jpg 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main-300x200.jpg 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main-768x512.jpg 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main.jpg 1440w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /></figure>

The isolated nature of the glacier and its marshy surroundings make approaching on foot almost impossible, but photographer Dani Guindo captured gorgeous aerial images of the glacier&#8217;s many rivulets ribboning about the landscape it&#8217;s carved. [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/guindo-5-1024x683.jpeg" title="Image by Dani Guindo." alt="Image by Dani Guindo." /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Iceland&#8217;s Múlajökull <a href="/tagged/glacier/">glacier</a> is prone to sudden <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surge_(glacier)">surges</a>, where rapid ice flow is interspersed between periods of quiescence or retreat. The isolated nature of the glacier and its marshy surroundings make approaching on foot almost impossible, but photographer Dani Guindo captured gorgeous aerial images of the glacier&#8217;s many rivulets ribboning about the landscape it&#8217;s carved. (Image credit: <a href="https://www.behance.net/daniguindo">D. Guindo</a>; via <a href="https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/03/dani-guindo-iceland-glaciers-landscape-photography/">Colossal</a>)</p>

		<item>
		<title>Convection Inside the Mantle</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/convection-inside-the-mantle/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/convection-inside-the-mantle/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[buoyancy]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[convection]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[geophysics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[mantle convection]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[seismic waves]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31424</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Most of what we know about Earth&#8217;s interior comes from observing how seismic waves&#8211;mostly from earthquakes&#8211;bounce around. As our observations have gotten better&#8211;more seisometers, better imaging techniques&#8211;scientists have identified two large anomalies sitting near the bottom of the mantle. Known as large low-velocity provinces, or LLVPs, these zones take up continent-sized areas beneath parts of [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Most of what we know about Earth&#8217;s interior comes from observing how <a href="/tagged/seismic-waves/">seismic waves</a>&#8211;mostly from earthquakes&#8211;bounce around. As our observations have gotten better&#8211;more seisometers, better imaging techniques&#8211;scientists have identified two large anomalies sitting near the bottom of the mantle. Known as large low-velocity provinces, or LLVPs, these zones take up continent-sized areas beneath parts of Africa and the Pacific. </p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img decoding="async" width="1024" height="318" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f1-1024x318.png" alt="Seismic waves show lower speeds in large, continent-sized zones that sit beneath Africa and the Pacific. These large low-velocity provinces (LLVPs) are outlined in red." class="wp-image-31426" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f1-1024x318.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f1-300x93.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f1-768x238.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f1-1536x477.png 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f1-2048x636.png 2048w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Seismic waves show lower speeds in large, continent-sized zones that sit beneath Africa and the Pacific. These large low-velocity provinces (LLVPs) are outlined in red.</figcaption></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The LLVPs are hot, which would normally make them <a href="/tagged/buoyancy">buoyant</a>, but their stationary nature suggests they are made up of extremely dense material. Narrow plumes of hot material make their way up from the LLVPs to form <a href="/tagged/volcano/">volcanic</a> hotspots like those that made the Hawaiian and <a href="/tagged/Galapagos/">Galapagos Islands</a>. Balancing that upward <a href="/tagged/convection/">convection</a> is the downward convection of former tectonic material carried into the mantle at <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subduction">subduction zones</a>. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">What the LLVPs are made of remains an active research question. <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06589-1">One suggestion</a> is that they contain remnants of Theia, the planet thought to have impacted the proto-Earth to form our Moon. (Image credits: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1063/pt.mzrx.ddag">E. Garnero and C. Richardson</a>; see also <a href="https://doi.org/10.1063/pt.mzrx.ddag">Physics Today</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1024" height="974" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f2-1024x974.png" alt="Illustration showing convection in the Earth's inner mantle. Former tectonic material subducts downward in dark blue zones. The large low-velocity provinces (LLVPs) are shown in orange. Hot-spot volcanic activity is seen at the surface (black triangles) above narrow plumes that lift material from the LLVPs toward the surface." class="wp-image-31425" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f2-1024x974.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f2-300x285.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f2-768x731.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f2-1536x1461.png 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/PTO.v77.i12.36_1.f2-2048x1948.png 2048w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Illustration showing convection in the Earth&#8217;s inner mantle. Former tectonic material subducts downward in dark blue zones. The large low-velocity provinces (LLVPs) are shown in orange. Hot-spot volcanic activity is seen at the surface (black triangles) above narrow plumes that lift material from the LLVPs toward the surface.</figcaption></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

		<item>
		<title>Even Penguins Love Bubbles</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/even-penguins-love-bubbles/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/even-penguins-love-bubbles/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 22 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[biology]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[penguins]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[soap bubbles]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31695</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Walter, a young African penguin at the New York Aquarium, loves soap bubbles. In fairness to Walter, so do most people I&#8217;ve met. There&#8217;s just something that feels a bit magical about these ephemeral rainbow spheres that pop at a (dry) touch. Bubbles owe their colors to thin film interference&#8211;the colors actually indicate how thick [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Walter, a young African penguin at the New York Aquarium, loves <a href="/tagged/soap-bubbles/">soap bubbles</a>. In fairness to Walter, so do most people I&#8217;ve met. There&#8217;s just something that feels a bit magical about these ephemeral rainbow spheres that pop at a (dry) touch. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Bubbles owe their colors to <a href="/tagged/interference/">thin film interference</a>&#8211;the colors actually indicate how thick the bubble film is&#8211;and their stability (and fast disintegration) to <a href="/tagged/surface-tension/">surface tension</a>. With <a href="/2025/05/soap-bubble-bonanza/">schlieren photography</a> or <a href="/2024/01/inside-a-soap-bubble/">flow visualization</a>, watching bubbles gets even cooler. Do you suppose a penguin would <a href="/2022/04/within-the-bubbles-pop/">appreciate bubbles popping at 50,000 fps</a>? (Image credit: <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DZxtZp-Ftn1/?hl=en">New York Aquarium</a>; via <a href="https://www.popsci.com/environment/walter-the-penguin-loves-popping-bubbles/?__readwiseLocation=">PopSci</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="748" height="835" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/penguin_bubbles_main.jpg" alt="Walter the African Penguin enjoys popping bubbles." class="wp-image-31697" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/penguin_bubbles_main.jpg 748w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/penguin_bubbles_main-269x300.jpg 269w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 748px) 100vw, 748px" /></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

			<slash:comments>1</slash:comments>

		<item>
		<title>Where Waves Carry Plastics</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/where-waves-carry-plastics/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/where-waves-carry-plastics/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[ocean waves]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[plastic pollution]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[stokes drift]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31590</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The classic theory of steady wave motion predicts a phenomenon called Stokes drift, in which particles spread horizontally in the direction of wave travel. That means that something like microplastics will drift in the direction that waves are traveling. But in the real world, ocean waves aren&#8217;t quite so neat and unchanging. A new study [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The classic theory of steady wave motion predicts a phenomenon called <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokes_drift">Stokes drift</a>, in which particles spread horizontally in the direction of wave travel. That means that something like microplastics will drift in the direction that waves are traveling. But in the real world, ocean waves aren&#8217;t quite so neat and unchanging. A <a href="https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/0295-5075/ae7abb#epl26100131s4">new study</a> looks at what happens when waves are decaying in strength&#8211;in other words, what happens in our world when the wind dies down.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In those circumstances, the researchers found that particles did not just drift horizontally&#8211;they drifted vertically, too. Further, how much a particle drifts vertically depends on its initial depth. Since plastics vary in their buoyancy&#8211;and can be found in varying numbers and sizes throughout the upper layer of the ocean&#8211;this mechanism could significantly affect how waves mix and transport pollution. (Image credit: <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/white-and-brown-boats-on-blue-sea-water-during-daytime-2St3S36Gu7w">N. Jensen</a>; research credit: <a href="https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/0295-5075/ae7abb#epl26100131s4">T. Izawa et al.</a>; via <a href="https://physicsworld.com/a/new-model-of-ocean-waves-sheds-fresh-light-on-the-spread-of-microplastic-pollution/?nbd_source=3626823&amp;__readwiseLocation=">Physics World</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>
					
					<wfw:commentRss>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/where-waves-carry-plastics/feed/</wfw:commentRss>
			<slash:comments>0</slash:comments>

		<item>
		<title>Making Quieter Shock Waves</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/making-quieter-shock-waves/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/making-quieter-shock-waves/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 20 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[schlieren photography]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[shockwave]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[supersonic]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[supersonic flight]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[supersonic wind tunnel]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[wind tunnel testing]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31735</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[NASA&#8217;s X-59 aircraft is intended to demonstrate supersonic flight without the boom. Although it&#8217;s broken into supersonic speeds, we haven&#8217;t yet heard its &#8220;sonic thump&#8221; because, so far, it&#8217;s been accompanied by conventional supersonic aircraft, which are louder. The idea behind the long, skinny X-59 is to create weaker, widely-spaced shocks along the aircraft body. [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">NASA&#8217;s X-59 aircraft is intended to demonstrate <a href="/tagged/supersonic/">supersonic</a> flight without the boom. Although it&#8217;s broken into supersonic speeds, we haven&#8217;t yet heard its &#8220;sonic thump&#8221; because, so far, it&#8217;s been accompanied by conventional supersonic aircraft, which are louder.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The idea behind the long, skinny X-59 is to create weaker, widely-spaced <a href="/tagged/shockwave/">shocks</a> along the aircraft body. Weaker shocks are easier for atmospheric effects to damp out before they reach the ground, and  spacing them out makes it harder for them to &#8220;pile up&#8221; at the nose and tail to create the strong double shocks that merge into a sonic boom.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-large"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1024" height="576" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/x59_shock-1024x576.png" alt="Schlieren image of a model X-59 tested at supersonic conditions in a wind tunnel." class="wp-image-31739" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/x59_shock-1024x576.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/x59_shock-300x169.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/x59_shock-768x432.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/x59_shock.png 1280w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Schlieren image of a model X-59 tested at supersonic conditions in a wind tunnel. The model is mounted upside-down. The three dark diagonal lines are shock waves originating from the wind tunnel and can be ignored. The fainter lines coming off parts of the aircraft model are the plane&#8217;s shock waves. </figcaption></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">NASA is preparing to test the X-59&#8217;s in-flight shocks soon, including with <a href="https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20210024873">in-air schlieren photography</a> like they&#8217;ve <a href="/2019/03/this-week-nasa-released-the-first-ever-image-of/">done in the past</a> for other aircraft. But we&#8217;ve already have a glimpse of what to expect, thanks to <a href="https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220010676">wind tunnel testing</a>, shown above. Ignore the three dark diagonal lines in the middle of the image (those are from the wind tunnel, not the model aircraft), and focus instead on the thin bright lines coming off the plane. Those are some impressively subtle shock waves! </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Hear more from the aircraft&#8217;s designer and test pilots in this <a href="https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/06/nasas-x-59-frankenjet-tests-supersonic-flight-without-the-sonic-boom/?__readwiseLocation=">Ars Technica article</a>. (Image credit: NASA; see also: <a href="https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/06/nasas-x-59-frankenjet-tests-supersonic-flight-without-the-sonic-boom/?__readwiseLocation=">Ars Technica</a>, <a href="https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220010676">M. Ahaus et al.</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>
					
					<wfw:commentRss>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/making-quieter-shock-waves/feed/</wfw:commentRss>
